actions.justification: Mandatory first step per WAO anaphylaxis guideline. Patient has dyspnea and hypotension — airway patency, breathing adequacy, and circulatory status must be immediately evaluated to guide urgency and treatment decisions.

Mandatory per WAO guideline. Patient meets clinical criteria: acute onset urticaria (skin involvement) + dyspnea (respiratory compromise) + hypotension (cardiovascular involvement). Formal assessment confirms anaphylaxis diagnosis to guide epinephrine administration.

Mandatory per WAO anaphylaxis guideline. Identifying and removing the causative trigger (e.g., stopping an IV infusion, removing a stinger) is a critical early step to halt ongoing allergen exposure and limit reaction progression.

Epinephrine IM is the first-line mandatory treatment for anaphylaxis per WAO guidelines. This patient meets anaphylaxis criteria (urticaria + dyspnea + hypotension). Must be given immediately — antihistamines are contraindicated as first-line.
IV access is mandatory for fluid resuscitation and medication delivery in anaphylaxis, especially given the patient's hypotension (MAP 60 mmHg).
Supine positioning with legs elevated improves venous return and supports blood pressure in anaphylaxis-related hypotension. Mandatory per anaphylaxis management guidelines.
Continuous cardiac and SpO2 monitoring is essential after epinephrine administration in anaphylaxis to detect biphasic reaction, arrhythmia, or hemodynamic deterioration.
High-flow oxygen is indicated in anaphylaxis with dyspnea and history of asthma to support oxygenation and address bronchospasm component, per WAO anaphylaxis guidelines.

Anaphylaxis with hypotension and respiratory involvement in an asthmatic patient warrants early escalation; additional personnel should be mobilized in case of rapid deterioration or need for advanced airway management.

After epinephrine IM administration, serial vital sign reassessment is critical to evaluate treatment response and detect biphasic anaphylaxis or persistent hypotension. Current MAP is borderline at 60 mmHg.

Patient has hypotension (MAP 60 mmHg) consistent with anaphylaxis-related vasodilation. IV fluid resuscitation with normal saline bolus is indicated as adjunct therapy after epinephrine per WAO anaphylaxis guidelines.

Corticosteroids are recommended in anaphylaxis management to reduce risk of biphasic or protracted reaction, particularly important given patient's comorbid asthma which increases risk of severe bronchospasm.
After epinephrine as first-line treatment, H1 antihistamines are indicated as adjunctive therapy to help relieve urticarial symptoms in anaphylaxis per WAO guidelines.
H2 antihistamines are recommended as adjunctive therapy alongside H1 antihistamines to provide more complete histamine blockade in anaphylaxis management.

Patient with anaphylaxis requires observation for at least 4 hours after epinephrine administration to monitor for biphasic anaphylaxis reaction. Given comorbid asthma, extended observation is warranted.

Serum tryptase should be drawn 1-3 hours after anaphylaxis onset to confirm mast cell activation and support the diagnosis of anaphylaxis. At 75 minutes post-presentation this is an appropriate time to collect the sample.

Patient has asthma (risk factor for severe/biphasic reaction) and had hypotension/respiratory symptoms. WAO guidelines recommend extended observation (minimum 8 hours) for patients with anaphylaxis and risk factors for biphasic reaction, even after apparent clinical recovery.

Patient has comorbid asthma and presented with dyspnea. Nebulized salbutamol (albuterol) is indicated as adjunct bronchodilator therapy for bronchospasm component in anaphylaxis with asthma, per WAO anaphylaxis guidelines.

Patient has asthma (high-risk comorbidity) increasing risk of biphasic anaphylaxis reaction. WAO guidelines recommend extended observation (minimum 24 hours) for high-risk patients after anaphylaxis. Previous observations (4h and 8h) are completed but 24h observation is warranted.
Per anaphylaxis management guidelines, patient education about identifying and avoiding triggers is essential before discharge to prevent recurrence.

WAO anaphylaxis guidelines strongly recommend prescribing an epinephrine autoinjector (e.g., EpiPen) to all patients who have experienced anaphylaxis, especially those with asthma as a comorbidity, for self-administration in case of future reactions.

Patient has asthma as comorbidity and presented with dyspnea. Despite clinical improvement, airway reassessment is critical to ensure no residual bronchospasm or angioedema risk, and to verify continued patency before considering disposition.
Per WAO anaphylaxis guidelines, patients should receive a written anaphylaxis action plan prior to discharge. This has not yet been completed and is essential for secondary prevention.

Patient with anaphylaxis and asthma comorbidity requires extended observation for biphasic reaction risk. Admission to observation unit supports the already-ordered 24-hour minimum observation period.
